intro: The oak at the corner of Louisiana's Old State Capitol grounds was already standing when the capitol went up beside it in 1847, and by one estimate it is nearly twice the building's age. It has outlasted the fire of 1862 and the government's move out in 1932, and it still shades the lawn by Repentance Park. Out on Highland Road, the LSU Hilltop Arboretum keeps its own great live oak at its centre, the one couples book for their weddings.
meta_description: Two live oaks in Baton Rouge: the oak older than the Old State Capitol it shades, and the wedding oak at the heart of LSU Hilltop Arboretum.
question_meta: Baton Rouge's oldest documented tree is the live oak at the Old State Capitol, put at 230 to 300 years. Where it stands, and one more worth the drive.
question_answer: The oldest documented tree in Baton Rouge is the live oak at the corner of the Old State Capitol grounds, beside Repentance Park on the downtown riverfront. Country Roads magazine puts it at roughly 300 years and about five metres round; a visitors' waymark says about 230. Neither comes from a ring count, but both put it ahead of the capitol, built between 1847 and 1849. The other great oak in town, the wedding tree at LSU Hilltop Arboretum, has no published age beyond the Live Oak Society's Centenarian class, a hundred years or more.
question_context: The two ages for the Old State Capitol oak, 230 and 300 years, are both estimates, and live oaks are hard to date. They grow fast when young and slow unpredictably later, so a girth of about five metres fits a wide range of ages. Either figure means the tree saw the capitol built, saw fire gut its interior in 1862, and saw the state government leave for the new capitol in 1932. It should not be confused with the Thomas Boyd oak at the new State Capitol, which fell in Hurricane Gustav in 2008. The Old State Capitol is now a museum, closed on Sundays and Mondays, and the oak stands on the grounds by Repentance Park, a short walk from the River Center. The second tree is a drive away, at LSU Hilltop Arboretum on Highland Road, open free every day in daylight. Its own university gives two different sizes for it, a diameter of 8 feet on one page and 17 on another, so its size is an open question. It is named for Emory Smith, who began the arboretum in 1929.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Baton Rouge?
faq.a: The live oak at the corner of the Old State Capitol grounds is the oldest with a published estimate, roughly 230 to 300 years depending on the source. Neither figure comes from a ring count.

faq.q: Is the Old State Capitol oak the one that fell in Hurricane Gustav?
faq.a: No. The oak lost in Gustav in 2008 was the Thomas Boyd oak at the new State Capitol. The Old State Capitol oak, by Repentance Park, still stands.

faq.q: Can you visit the wedding tree at Hilltop Arboretum?
faq.a: Yes. LSU Hilltop Arboretum on Highland Road is open to the public free of charge during daylight hours, seven days a week. The tree is the arboretum's focal point, and the office, open Tuesday to Friday, can point you to it.

trees.name: Old State Capitol Oak

location.address: Louisiana Old State Capitol grounds, 100 North Boulevard, Baton Rouge, LA 70801 (corner of the property beside Repentance Park)

trees.story:
By one estimate this live oak is nearly twice as old as the building it shades, and the building is Louisiana's Old State Capitol.

Country Roads magazine puts the tree at roughly 300 years and about 16 feet around the trunk, close to five metres. A waymark posted by visitors in 2009 says about 230. Neither comes from a ring count, so take it as somewhere between the two. Either way the oak was here first. The capitol went up beside it between 1847 and 1849.

That means it has stood through everything the building has. Fire gutted the capitol's interior in 1862, during the Civil War. It was rebuilt and reopened in 1882, and in 1932 the state government moved out to its new capitol up the road, leaving the old one to become the museum it is today. Through all of it the oak kept its corner of the grounds, by what is now Repentance Park on the downtown riverfront.

Do not confuse it with the Thomas Boyd oak at the new State Capitol, which came down in Hurricane Gustav in 2008. That one is gone. This one still shades the lawn, a short walk from the River Center.

The museum closes on Sundays and Mondays, and the grounds' own hours are not posted, so the easiest time to come is a weekday.
trees.access: Grounds of the Louisiana Old State Capitol beside Repentance Park, on the downtown riverfront. The museum is closed Sunday and Monday; grounds hours are not posted.
trees.transport: Downtown Baton Rouge, on foot from the riverfront and the River Center. Bus stop not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big live oak at the corner of the Old State Capitol grounds, a trunk about five metres round. It stands on the side of the grounds next to Repentance Park.

Girth_cm 490 is 16 ft converted; the page says 'around the trunk' so it is read as circumference. Waymarking WM74T9 (posted 2009, 'Old Capitol Bicentennial Oak') gives age approx 230 years and coordinates 30 26.805 N, 091 11.327 W, and says the tree witnessed construction from 1847, the 1862 interior fire, the 1882 reopening and the 1932 move of the capitol; the Waymarking history is community-written, not a source. Ages conflict (230 vs 300), both are unmeasured estimates, no ring count. trees.name: Mr. Emory Wedding Tree

location.address: LSU Hilltop Arboretum, 11855 Highland Road, Baton Rouge, LA 70810

trees.story:
LSU cannot agree with itself on how big this oak is. One page of the university's Hilltop Arboretum gives it a diameter of 8 feet, another a diameter of 17 feet, and one tree cannot be both. Seventeen feet would make more sense as the distance around the trunk, but nobody has published a fresh measurement to settle it.

What everyone agrees on is that it is the heart of the place. The arboretum calls it its focal point, and it is a favourite spot for weddings, which is half of its name. The other half honours Emory Smith, who began developing this hilltop off Highland Road in 1929 and gave it to LSU in 1981. What was his garden is now open to anyone, free, every day in daylight.

The Live Oak Society, the register of great live oaks kept by the Louisiana Garden Club Federation, lists it in its Centenarian class, which by the Society's reckoning means a tree of about a hundred years or more. Beyond that nobody has put a date on it, and with two sizes in circulation a girth estimate would only add a third guess. If you know how old it is, tell us.

The arboretum is a walk-through garden in south Baton Rouge, reached by car, and the office is staffed from Tuesday to Friday if you need directions to the tree.
trees.access: LSU Hilltop Arboretum is open to the public free of charge during daylight hours, seven days a week; the office is open 9 to 4:30, Tuesday to Friday.
trees.transport: Highland Road, south of the LSU campus, reached by car. No practical public transport found.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the arboretum's focal point, the big live oak where weddings are held. It stands in LSU Hilltop Arboretum off Highland Road; the office, open Tuesday to Friday, can point you to it.
trees.verify_notes: FLAGGED: the ground's owner (LSU) is the only source and the sizes conflict. LSU's own pages call it the focal point of the arboretum and a favourite wedding site, a member of the Live Oak Society of the Louisiana Garden Club Federation in the Centenarian Trees classification, named in memory of donor Emory Smith, who began developing the arboretum in 1929 and gave it to LSU in 1981. The about page gives the tree 'a diameter of 8 feet' and the rental page 'a diameter of 17 feet'. 17 ft is plausibly a circumference (the Society treats 17 ft circumference as roughly 100 years); 8 ft is the Society's minimum girth. No girth_cm recorded because the figures conflict. age_min 100 is derived from the Society's Centenarian class only, age_max is a loose bound, no source states an age. Pin is the arboretum centroid from Wikipedia (30.35636, -91.09486), not the tree; the arboretum is a walk-through garden so no small-site claim. lifecheck.py at the centroid: RECENT, iNaturalist 2026-10-17 (garden-level, not this trunk). Alive-now for this individual tree is not shown by a dated photo; an LSU page still presents it as a focal point.
